posts.title: Inside batch 112: a week at the still
posts.excerpt: A day-by-day account of how batch 112 moved through our copper pot still Ottilie over nine quiet days in Larchmere.
posts.content:
The copper kettle of our three-hundred-litre pot still, Ottilie, holds the quiet heart of our distillery on Quarry Lane. It is Wednesday morning in Larchmere, marking day four of nine for batch one hundred and twelve. Outside the timber doors, maritime mist hangs low over the harbour water, but inside the still room, the air is warm with the sharp resin of wild juniper berries and sweet steamed citrus. This batch began on Sunday when botanical forager Inès Dubreuil and head distiller Mira Okafor weighed our botanical charge, preparing nine ingredients for their measured cycle of distillation. Each basket of dried roots, citrus peel, and whole spices was checked by hand before entering the copper vessel.

Every batch at Taruki follows the identical six stages we established in 2016: botanicals, steep, still, cut, rest, and bottle. For batch one hundred and twelve, citrus grower Samir Haddad delivered freshly harvested lemon and bitter orange rinds from the Hillside Grove. The thick, fragrant peels were arranged on slatted timber trays alongside cracked coriander seeds, angelica root, and coastal sea fennel. Once weighed, the base botanicals steeped in neutral spirit within our maceration vessel, allowing dense roots to yield their grounding oils before heat touched the kettle.

By Tuesday, still operator Tomasz Wren had transferred the steeped spirit into Ottilie, firing the boiler at a measured, unhurried pace. We deliberately run Ottilie slowly. Rushing distillation overheats the copper, scorching delicate aromatic compounds and introducing harsh vegetal notes. Instead, gentle steam coaxed vapour upward through the tall copper swan neck throughout the distillation run. Copper strips away sulphur compounds, refining the mouthfeel of the vapour before it meets the cold coils of the condenser and turns to liquid spirit. Tomasz kept vigil beside the gauges, adjusting the heat to maintain a steady, gentle trickle of spirit.

Today marks the pivotal cut stage. Mira stands beside Ottilie's collection spout with a small glass, evaluating spirit density and aroma at short intervals. The volatile heads, pungent with harsh solvent notes, have already been discarded. Now, the pure heart of the distillation run flows in a thin, glass-clear stream. Mira dips her glass, dilutes a droplet with water, and tastes. The palate reveals bright lemon peel and pine resin, grounded by the earthy sweetness of angelica and the faint saline mineral note of sea fennel. This balanced spirit represents the true character of our harbour town.

By late afternoon, the sensory profile shifts toward the oily, heavier tails, and Mira closes the heart receiver. Batch one hundred and twelve will now rest in stainless steel conditioning tanks for several days. This resting stage permits ethanol molecules and botanical essential oils to marry into a cohesive, velvety spirit. Later this week, bottling lead Ruth Abernathy will bring the liquid to bottling proof with pure water, fill each glass bottle by hand, and press a wood-topped cork into the neck. Exactly four hundred and twenty bottles will emerge from batch one hundred and twelve, each numbered by hand and ready for our tasting room bar. Visitors arriving for our weekend tours will taste the culmination of this patient nine-day cycle.

posts.title: Why Ottilie runs slowly
posts.excerpt: How gentle copper temperatures keep the subtle citrus notes.
posts.content:
Ottilie is a 300-litre copper pot still, and we run her gently. Low steam keeps the delicate oils in the juniper, coriander and citrus peel from scorching, and the long contact with the copper dome cleans the vapour.

A faster run would be cheaper. It would also taste flatter. So we keep the nine-day cycle and let the still take its time.

posts.title: Peel from the Hillside Grove
posts.excerpt: Partnering with Samir Haddad for fresh orchard fruit.
posts.content:
In 2019 Mira began buying peel from Samir Haddad, who tends lemon and bitter orange trees on the hill above Larchmere. The fruit is hand-harvested, and the peel is pared thin the same day.

It changed the gin. The lemon is brighter, the bitter orange rounder, and the sea air of the hillside is in the glass.
